title: Leapfrogging cancer diagnostics with AI: a mixed-methods assessment of implementation determinants in low- and middle-income countries
abstract: Introduction Cancer incidence is rising rapidly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where diagnostic pathology capacity is constrained. AI applied to routine histopathology could strengthen diagnostic capacity and offer leapfrogging potential by embedding AI into diagnostic systems as they are built up. However, without empirically identifying implementation determinants in LMIC cancer-diagnostic settings, AI solutions risk being poorly aligned with local constraints, limiting impact or exacerbating existing disparities. Methods We conducted an exploratory mixed-methods pilot study across three phases: 1) a structured survey characterising the diagnostic and technical landscape and AI priorities; 2) focus group discussions (FGDs) to inductively identify implementation determinants and 3) a second survey quantifying FGD-derived themes. Twelve physicians were purposively recruited (10 from LMIC, 2 from high-income countries for reference) and findings integrated through narrative triangulation. Results There was substantial heterogeneity in diagnostic and AI infrastructure that did not track consistently with country income classification. H&E staining was universally available, immunohistochemistry capacity was rudimentary at 7 of 10 sites and molecular testing absent or minimal at 6 of 10 sites. Whole-slide-imaging scanners were available at 8 of 10 sites, while graphical processing units, required for efficient AI inference, were available at only 4 of 10 sites. The participants would prioritise use of AI for cancer screening, cancer diagnosis, and biomarker prediction from H&E slides. Six implementation determinants were identified: AI literacy, governance frameworks, funding, evidence generation, clinical deployment, and collaboration. Financial constraints emerged as the dominant barrier across all determinants, and collaboration as an important enabling mechanism. Conclusion AI implementation readiness in LMIC cancer-diagnostic settings is highly heterogeneous and cannot be inferred from income classification, underscoring the need for institution-level assessment. Realising the leapfrogging potential of AI in this context requires coordinated progress across all determinants, with sustainable financing, and collaboration enabling the remaining determinants. Key messages What is already known on this topic? Cancer incidence is rising rapidly in LMICs, where diagnostic capacity and molecular testing capabilities are severely constrained. AI could alleviate gaps, yet evidence on implementation determinants for integrating AI into cancer diagnostics in these settings remains limited. What this study adds? AI implementation readiness varies substantially within LMIC settings and does not track with country income classification. Readiness is shaped by six implementation determinants: AI literacy, governance frameworks, funding, evidence generation, clinical deployment, and collaboration, with financial constraints as the dominant cross-cutting barrier. How this study might affect research, practice or policy? These findings support institution-level feasibility assessment over income-classification proxies and highlight the need for sustainable financing and collaboration as foundational prerequisites for AI implementation in cancer diagnostics in LMICs.

title: Optogenetic and sonogenetic pacing of unmodified cardiac tissue upon quick integration with specialized biological actuators
abstract: ABSTRACT Electrical stimulation for cardiac pacing has been in clinical use for 100 years and it is the current standard. Alternative scalable pacing methods that are contactless, with good spatial precision and can also be cell-selective are of interest for both in vitro and in vivo applications. Cardiac pacing by light or by ultrasound (US) can be achieved using optogenetic transduction of the tissue and by enhancing responsiveness to ultrasound. In this work we create specialized biological actuators (cell spheroids) out of generic human cells, modified optogenetically (using Channelrhodopsin2) and sonogenetically (using human Piezo1), guide them to a desired location to promote quick integration with unmodified cardiac syncytia within less than two hours. We quantify their ability to confer pacing by light or US and to entrain the native cardiac tissue, modeled here with human induced pluripotent stem cell derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) grown in monolayers, quasi-3D oriented microtissues or cell spheroids. Magnetic guidance (via magnetic nanoparticles) speeds up integration and facilitates positioning to optimize electrotonic load for pacing; size match and three-dimensional growth also accelerate integration. Computational modeling corroborates the possibility to pace by light and by US. Using optogenetically-gated US pulses (0.5 MHz), we show entrainment in voltage and calcium responses and identify the best performing configurations. Experiments reveal the potential role of Piezo1, esp. when activated with Yoda1. The approach is shown to work with physiologically relevant heart cells, such as human cardiac fibroblasts as optimized actuators, and therefore can be considered for in vivo applications as part of heart regeneration efforts. High-throughput cardiotoxicity testing and drug screening in vitro can directly benefit from deployment of such biological actuators.

title: Overuse and False Restraint in Large Language Model Recommendations for Choosing Wisely Scenarios.
abstract: Background The Choosing Wisely initiative made recommendations where screening, testing, or treatment may be overused, with caveats around appropriate use. Clinicians are increasingly using large language models (LLMs). Objective To evaluate whether commercial LLMs appropriately call for restraint or action from scenarios based on Choosing Wisely recommendations. Design Benchmark evaluation. Fifteen Choosing Wisely recommendations were used to develop 225 scenarios (per recommendation, 10 in which restraint was appropriate and 5 in which action was appropriate). Six commercial LLMs (3 runs each) generated 4050 responses to the 225 scenarios, using a prompt from the clinician perspective. Setting Production application programming interfaces of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google from February to March 2026. Participants No human participants were involved. Measurements Co-primary outcomes were the overuse rate (endorsing action when restraint was appropriate) and the false restraint rate (withholding an appropriate action). Results The rate of LLM-recommended overuse was 5.4% (95% CI, 0.6% to 12.2%); LLMs did not recommend overuse in 8 of 15 recommendations. Two recommendations accounted for most LLM-recommended overuse: thyroid ultrasound for an incidental subcentimeter nodule (overuse recommended in 42.8% of LLM responses) and routine electrocardiography in low-risk adults (overuse recommended in 28.3% of LLM responses). The LLMs recommended overuse in 0.6% to 3.3% of responses for the remaining 5 recommendations. False restraint was rare (0.6% [CI, 0.1% to 1.2%]), was absent for 11 of 15 recommendations, and was highest for prostate-specific antigen screening (3.3%). Limitations Single prompts without follow-up; a benchmark rather than real-world use; responses classified by LLM judge with physician adjudication. Findings may not extend to consumer-facing use. Conclusion The LLMs rarely withheld recommendations for treatment when it was appropriate. Overuse was concentrated in 2 recommendations. Primary funding source None.

title: Diffuse-Type Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor of the Flexor Hallucis Longus Tendon Sheath: A Case Report.
abstract: The synovium can be the primary site for the development of various benign or malignant tumors. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT), also known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath, is a benign but locally aggressive synovial neoplasm occurring in localized and diffuse forms. The localized form predominantly affects the hand, whereas the diffuse form mainly involves large joints; involvement of the flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath is rare. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the principal modality for demonstrating the hemosiderin deposits characteristic of this lesion, although histopathology remains necessary for definitive diagnosis. Surgical resection remains the standard treatment. We report the case of a 24-year-old man with 10 months of right ankle pain, related to a diffuse-type TGCT involving the flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath and adjacent ankle joints. Radiographs initially showed soft-tissue filling of Kager's triangle. Computed tomography arthrography demonstrated synovial thickening but was nonspecific; MRI then revealed the characteristic findings, and histopathology confirmed the diagnosis. This report aims to raise awareness of this rare location and its associated diagnostic pitfalls.

title: ACorD: Adaptive Correspondence Discovery for Medical Image Registration
abstract: Medical image registration is a fundamental task for aligning anatomical structures across images. Exhaustively searching for point-wise correspondences is prohibitively expensive in both computation and memory, particularly for high-resolution 3D medical images. Most recent learning-based methods directly predict correspondences in a coarse-to-fine manner, but often propagate intermediate estimates across scales without explicitly weighting correspondence evidence, which can allow coarse-scale errors to persist during refinement. To address these challenges, we propose ACorD, an adaptive correspondence discovery framework designed to mitigate error propagation with an attention-guided process. ACorD first predicts multiple potential correspondence candidates through Correlation-guided Cross-scale Offset Prediction (CCOP), which combines correlation maps as spatial matching priors with cross-scale features as global deformation context. Then, Multi-Head Deformable Aggregation (MHDA) aggregates these candidate correspondences using attention, producing a learned, non-uniform weighting over competing matches rather than treating them equally. The multi-head design further captures complementary deformation patterns, ensuring both global alignment and local precision. By integrating adaptive offset prediction with selective, attention-based aggregation of correspondence evidence, ACorD enables accurate deformation refinement. Extensive experiments on four public medical registration benchmarks demonstrate that adaptive correspondence discovery within a multi-scale refinement framework improves registration robustness across diverse anatomical structures.

title: Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient MCI Conversion Prediction
abstract: Allocating limited trainable capacity across convolutional layers is a central challenge in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of pretrained three-dimensional (3D) networks. We propose Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation, which jointly selects input- and output-channel ranks under a fixed adapter-parameter budget while preserving the spatial kernel modes. To guide rank selection, we learn task-specific proxy updates from downstream training data and approximate them using candidate Tucker rank pairs. A perturbation analysis bounds the output discrepancy between the fixed proxy network and its Tucker approximation in terms of layerwise reconstruction residuals, motivating residual-based allocation. We normalize each squared residual by the corresponding proxy-update energy to compare relative approximation errors across layers. Dynamic programming minimizes their sum under a global budget constraint that accounts for both channel factors and the Tucker core. This yields a globally optimal allocation over the specified candidate rank pairs. We evaluate the method on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort for predicting conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease within 36 months, using hippocampal segmentation pretraining. Across five random seeds, the proposed method achieves a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.7706, compared with 0.7239 for fixed-ratio Tucker adaptation and 0.7430 for full fine-tuning. The total number of trainable parameters is limited to approximately 0.618 million, accounting for only 1.45% of the full model. Adaptive Tucker rank allocation thus provides an effective approach to parameter-efficient transfer learning in 3D medical imaging.

title: How Robust Are Prognostic Radiomic Features? Comparing Selection Techniques on Pooled Glioblastoma Cohorts
abstract: Radiomic survival studies in glioblastoma report heterogeneous prognostic features, but how much of this stems from the methodology itself is rarely examined. We analysed the association of 463 radiomic, anatomical and clinical features from pre-treatment MRI with overall survival in 705 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma patients from three public cohorts, using three techniques: a log-rank test after median split, univariate Cox regression (both Benjamini-Hochberg corrected) and an XGBoost regressor interpreted with SHAP. The log-rank test selected 99 features, Cox regression 72 and SHAP its top 20; five were selected by all three: age, a peritumoural T2 texture feature, the number of connected peritumoural mask components and two image-level intensity maxima. The two survival tests shared 51 features, about half of the SHAP top 20 were also selected by either test, and where selections overlapped, effect directions agreed. Many selections were PyRadiomics diagnostic descriptors that are not restricted to tumour voxels. Analytical pipeline choices, including ranking method, pre-filtering and descriptor handling, can substantially influence which features appear prognostic.

title: XGLASS: X-Ray, Gaze and Language Assisted Slice Sequencing for CT Volumes
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) achieve remarkable performance on 2D medical images, such as X-rays or pathology images, while 3D VLMs that directly process CT/MRI volumes lag behind due to limited 3D training data and the predominance of 2D foundation architectures. To leverage powerful 2D VLMs for analyzing medical volumes, which contain hundreds of slices, it is therefore necessary to focus only on those few slices, which are diagnostically relevant. To enable such a prioritization, we propose XGLASS, a method that transfers medical expertise from 2D X-rays to 3D CT for task-aware slice prioritization. XGLASS uses disease-conditioned importance maps derived from language-aligned radiologist gaze on X-rays and spatially aligns them with coronal CT projections, bringing gaze priors and CT content into a shared 2D representation. The fused gaze-prior/CT projection is then used to predict a disease-specific ordering of axial slices, prioritizing diagnostically relevant slices. XGLASS significantly improves budgeted retrieval over 2D and 3D-native baselines, achieving a top-10 hit rate up to 75.9% for the best-performing disease. In practice, this means that after inspecting only the top 10 slices (4.17% of a 240-slice scan), XGLASS identifies a diagnostically relevant slice in more than 75% of cases. For downstream slice-wise finding classification, an XGLASS-selected 30-slice candidate set reduces model calls by 87.5% while improving F1 by 11.3 percentage points over all-slice inference, 4.2 points over the strongest 2D selector, and remains competitive with 3D-native selectors while requiring up to 130.8 times less time and 10.9 times less GPU memory per finding, supporting its use as a lightweight preselector for volumetric CT analysis. The code and pretrained checkpoint are available on https://github.com/michaelgloeckler/XGLASS.

title: TIM: Temporal Decoupling with Iterative Mutual-Refinement Model for Longitudinal Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) aims to translate medical images into diagnostic text, reducing radiologists' workload and standardizing clinical documentation. Nonetheless, existing approaches mainly focus on single-timepoint analysis and fail to capture temporal disease evolution across longitudinal examinations. While recent longitudinal RRG (LRRG) approaches incorporate historical data, they often combine images from different time points within a single representation space, leading to blurred semantics and inconsistent temporal reasoning. In this work, we propose a Temporal Decoupling with Iterative Mutual-Refinement Model (TIM), a two-stage framework that explicitly decouples spatial pathology from temporal progression and iteratively refines reports through mutual feedback. Stage I performs temporal-decoupled representation learning, separating temporal evolution patterns from disease-specific features and generating radiology reports for both prior and current studies. Stage II introduces a mutual report refinement mechanism that identifies diagnostic inconsistencies within prior reports and iteratively rectifies both prior and current reports through error-sensitive feedback. Experiments on the Longitudinal-MIMIC dataset demonstrate that TIM surpasses existing single-image and longitudinal baselines, achieving new state-of-the-art performance across both language and clinical metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/yihengd/TIM.

title: MCDA: Multi-View Graph Contrastive Learning with Dynamic Topology Augmentation for Functional MRI Analysis
abstract: Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) is a vital non-invasive tool for diagnosing brain disorders and uncovering pathological mechanisms. However, existing graph contrastive learning (GCL) methods often underexploit augmentation histories across training epochs and the relationships among different augmented views. In this paper, we introduce a topology-guided Multi-view graph Contrastive learning framework with Dynamic graph topology Augmentation (MCDA) for fMRI analysis. Unlike traditional GCL that uses fixed noise or edge-dropping, MCDA employs a Dynamic Augmentation Update (DAU) module that iteratively refines the augmented topology. Specifically, we incorporate self-aware and cross-sample augmentation strategies to simultaneously capture individual-specific functional signatures and inter-subject heterogeneity. We then design a topology-guided multi-view graph contrastive learning scheme that explores interrelationships not only between the original network and its augmented views, but also across different augmented views to maximize structural information preservation. We characterize the score-level optimization directions and establish a lower bound for the contrastive objective. The framework combines classification and contrastive losses for brain disorder diagnosis and examines discriminative functional connectivity patterns as potential biomarkers. Experiments on two public rs-fMRI datasets comprising 1,236 subjects demonstrate that MCDA outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. The code has been made publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/goodcodingagoodboy/MCDA}.

title: HGASurv: Hierarchical Granularity-Aware Multimodal Integration for Survival Prediction
abstract: Multimodal survival prediction jointly analyzes histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs), genomic profiles, and clinical variables to stratify patients by risk. However, existing approaches often inadequately account for granularity differences across modalities, particularly in spatial organization and feature dimensionality. Within pathology, aggregating WSI patch features without preserving their spatial arrangement can obscure tissue architecture; across modalities, directly concatenating low-dimensional clinical variables with high-dimensional visual and genomic features may limit the contribution of clinical information to prediction. To address these challenges, we propose HGASurv, which introduces a hierarchical WSI encoding module and a clinical-guided graph propagation module for granularity-aware multimodal integration. The hierarchical WSI encoding module maps WSI patch features onto a spatial grid using their original coordinates and applies parallel convolutions to construct representations at patch, local-neighborhood, and regional scales. Genomic signature embeddings then query these scale-specific WSI representations through cross-modal co-attention, producing signature-conditioned morphological features. The clinical-guided graph propagation module uses clinical variables to define patient-similarity edges and propagates fused image-genomic node embeddings with graph attention, integrating clinical information through topology rather than feature concatenation. Across three TCGA cohorts, HGASurv achieved the strongest overall C-index performance, with ablation studies supporting the complementary contributions of the hierarchical WSI encoding and clinical-guided graph propagation modules. This design shows that matching representation and integration mechanisms to modality-specific granularity improves multimodal survival prediction.

title: Progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory for incomplete multimodal brain tumor segmentation
abstract: Brain tumor segmentation uses complementary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequences, but some sequences may be unavailable in practice. Their absence changes the information available for segmenting different tumor regions. Fusion methods can support different input subsets. However, fusion at several scales does not by itself specify how tumor evidence is retained and updated to guide fusion at later stages. We propose a progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory network (PMTM) for segmentation from any non-empty subset of T1ce, T1, FLAIR, and T2. PMTM maintains a compact state for the current subject across the encoder stages. At each stage, we use assignment maps to pool spatial features into ordered evidence vectors for each available modality. We average these vectors across the available modalities, and a learned gate combines this evidence with the previous state. The up- dated state guides residual fusion at that stage and is used in the state update at the next stage. A modality-token mixer also models interactions among the available modalities at each stage. We apply semantic supervision to the assignment maps at all four stages. We evaluate PMTM on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI across all 15 non-empty modality subsets. Averaged over the three tumor regions and the 15 subsets, PMTM achieves Dice scores of 75.31%, 77.54%, and 80.47% on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI, respectively. These scores are higher than those of RobustSeg, RFNet, and mmFormer in our experiments on each dataset. Component ablations and internal state analysis are performed on BraTS2020.

title: 3D Diffusion Models for Medical Imaging
abstract: Generative deep learning methods such as Variational Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks or Diffusion Models have achieved remarkable results in image synthesis. In particular, Diffusion Models have demonstrated superior image fidelity and sample diversity compared to other approaches on standard benchmarks, while also offering more flexible training dynamics as evidenced both in natural image domains and in medical applications. In medical imaging including Computed Tomography, Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Positron Emission Tomography, such models have various important use-cases including data augmentation, domain transfer, image reconstruction, inpainting, image augmentation and artifact correction. Further, generated images can be conditioned on patient characteristics, medical reports, segmentation masks or other images. Specific challenges arise due to the 3D volumetric nature of medical images, which translate to substantial demands in terms of memory, compute, and training data. This article provides a comparative overview of 3D Diffusion Models which have been developed for medical images, with a focus on current performance, limitations, and an outlook for future work.

title: MRI Reconstruction Risk Estimation from Inference Dynamics
abstract: Iterative MRI reconstructors produce intermediate estimates before returning a final image. We study these inference trajectories as a model-internal representation of realized reconstruction risk, measured by log-NMSE. Model-native states are projected to magnitude images, summarized by a fixed 16-dimensional descriptor, and mapped to risk using a source-trained ridge readout. Across three reconstruction backbones, trajectory features are strongly predictive of reconstruction risk on held-out source data. Under zero-shot target shift, their behavior is backbone-dependent, exhibiting both preserved positive association and readout reversal. Conditional analyses show that trajectory information can remain associated with error beyond an initialization-only predictor. A prefix analysis further shows that useful trajectory information can emerge before reconstruction completes. Repeated-mask and low-shot calibration studies indicate that trajectories primarily encode persistent case difficulty, while their orientation and calibration can change under domain shift.

title: Scaling Vision Foundation Models for Toxicologic Pathology
abstract: Here, we present TOX-FM, a family of non-clinical PFMs trained on large-scale diverse histopathology datasets of over one million whole slide images consisting of over 60 organs across six animal species from over 14,000 toxicology studies across six decades. We introduce a comprehensive benchmark of 18 non-clinical downstream tasks, incorporate an established benchmark of 9 clinical downstream tasks, and evaluate TOX-FM against state-of-the-art clinical PFMs across both non-clinical and clinical domains. Notably, we explore open questions surrounding domain-specific training and cross-domain generalization, offering insights into the opportunities and challenges of applying PFMs in the non-clinical domain.

title: REST: Reliability-Guided Spatial Transcriptomics Supervision for Gene Expression Prediction from Histopathological HE-Stained Images
abstract: Histopathology is central to cancer diagnosis, but morphology in Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE)-stained images does not directly reveal the molecular states that characterize disease heterogeneity and inform tumor characterization, prognostic assessment, and biomarker discovery. Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) measures spatially resolved gene expression, providing molecular information within tissue architecture, yet differences in assay coverage and spot informativeness make paired HE--ST observations unequally reliable for representation learning. We propose Reliability-Guided Spatial Transcriptomics (REST) supervision with Biological Program Bank (BPB), a program-structured and reliability-guided ST-supervised training framework for predicting molecular information from H\&E images. REST constructs BPB from curated signature, pathway, and cell-type gene sets to provide a shared structure for ST encoding, reliability estimation, and molecular reconstruction. Guided by BPB, Spot-Reliability Contrastive Alignment (SRCA) measures the reliability of each spot from assay-level program coverage and spot-level activity dispersion, and reweights HE--ST alignment accordingly. Biology-Informed Program Reconstruction (BIPR) further uses learnable program queries to reconstruct member-gene expression from histological morphology. REST's training corpus comprised 209 samples (407,475 spots across 16 organs); evaluation used 70 disjoint samples (230,056 spots across eight organs) for gene-expression, pathway-activity, and cell-signature prediction. REST achieved the highest Macro correlation among state-of-the-art ST-supervised training methods and outperformed existing pathology foundation models. Code is available at https://github.com/lanfz2000/REST.

We propose Reliability-Guided Spatial Transcriptomics (REST) supervision with Biological Program Bank (BPB), a program-structured and reliability-guided ST-supervised training framework for predicting molecular information from H\&E images. REST constructs BPB from curated signature, pathway, and cell-type gene sets to provide a shared structure for ST encoding, reliability estimation, and molecular reconstruction. Guided by BPB, Spot-Reliability Contrastive Alignment (SRCA) measures the reliability of each spot from assay-level program coverage and spot-level activity dispersion, and reweights HE--ST alignment accordingly. Biology-Informed Program Reconstruction (BIPR) further uses learnable program queries to reconstruct member-gene expression from histological morphology. REST's training corpus comprised 209 samples (407,475 spots across 16 organs); evaluation used 70 disjoint samples (230,056 spots across eight organs) for gene-expression, pathway-activity, and cell-signature prediction. title: MoSAIK: Motion Search with Artificial Intelligence in K-space
abstract: Object: Motion artefacts remain a major limitation of routine two-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) brain MRI, reducing diagnostic confidence and often necessitating repeated acquisitions. MoSAIK (Motion Search with AI in K-space) retrospectively estimates in-plane rigid-body motion directly from standard multi-coil TSE k-space. Without a motion-free reference, external navigators, or additional acquisitions, MoSAIK infers motion from k-space self-consistency violations and incorporates predicted parameters into model-based, motion-aware reconstruction rather than synthesizing corrected images. Materials and Methods: Selected complex coil data were represented as log-magnitude and phase channels. A decoupled convolutional embedding and Transformer encoder estimated phase-encoding-line-indexed rotation and two-dimensional translations. Training used motion-free clinical acquisitions with simulated motion; four held-out subjects were evaluated. Component-wise errors assessed estimation; SSIM and PSNR in silico and entropy focus criterion (EFC) in vivo assessed reconstruction. Results: Motion estimation errors were low for both rotation (MSE $<$ 0.2 deg$^2$) and translation (MSE $<$ 0.2 pixels$^2$), with Pearson correlations of approximately 0.96 and 0.94, respectively. In every in-vivo acquisition, more than 75% of slices showed information gain relative to uncorrected reconstructions. MoSAIK reduced visible artefacts while preserving anatomical detail. Discussion: Transformer-based k-space motion-trajectory estimation enables fast retrospective correction of standard clinical TSE brain MRI.

title: Computer-Assisted Hip Arthroscopy for Portal Establishment and Suture Anchor Placement.
abstract: Hip arthroscopy is the gold standard for treating femoroacetabular impingement syndrome and acetabular labral tears. Portal establishment and suture anchor placement are crucial steps for ensuring the success of the surgery. However, because of the complex anatomy, deep location, and narrow joint space of the hip joint, the learning curve for establishing the hip arthroscopy approach and placing suture anchors for labral repair is arduous, with a high risk of iatrogenic cartilage and labral damage. This article describes a solution that applies computer-assisted navigation to these 2 key steps. Based on the patient's preoperative computed tomography data, this technique enables the reconstruction of an individualized 3-dimensional skeletal model, on which the clockface target of the anterolateral portal at the acetabular rim and the placement sites of suture anchors for labral repair are precisely planned. Intraoperatively, high-precision spatial registration between the preoperative virtual plan and the patient's actual anatomical structure is achieved via 2-dimensional to 3-dimensional image registration. With the assistance of the navigation system, the surgeon can accurately establish the arthroscopic portal in a single attempt without fluoroscopy and safely perform acetabular suture anchor placement for subsequent labral suture.

title: Retained Colorectal Foreign Body After Suspected Chemical Incapacitation: A Surgical and Forensic Challenge.
abstract: Retained rectal foreign bodies are an uncommon but clinically significant surgical emergency. We report the case of a 74-year-old male with multiple medical comorbidities who presented with progressive rectal pain and obstipation several days after an episode of suspected drug-facilitated assault. Plain radiography identified a large metallic aerosol can, and attempts to retrieve it under general anesthesia using surgical clamps and a magnetic probe failed. Intraoperative fluoroscopy demonstrated that the can had migrated proximal to the rectosigmoid junction into the left colon, precluding transanal extraction. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy with longitudinal colotomy, permitting safe removal of the foreign body without evidence of perforation or visceral injury. This case illustrates the critical role of intraoperative fluoroscopy when digital examination fails, the indications for operative intervention in proximally migrated foreign bodies, and the importance of considering drug-facilitated assault as an etiology.

title: Progressive Hippocampal Volume Reduction Beyond Normal Aging in Temporal Lobe Epilepsy: A Longitudinal MRI Study.
abstract: Recent neuroimaging studies have suggested that epilepsy may show progressive brain structural changes over time. However, longitudinal hippocampal volume changes in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) have not been adequately compared with those observed in normal aging. In this study, we enrolled 46 patients with unilateral TLE and 25 healthy controls with longitudinal structural MRI scans using the same scanner. Hippocampal volumes were quantified using the Hipposeg software, and the annual percentage volume reduction relative to baseline (%Reduction/year) was calculated for each hippocampus. Compared to healthy hippocampi (median -0.37% per year, IQR = 3.97), both ipsilateral (median -1.04% per year, IQR = 3.65) and contralateral (median -1.08% per year, IQR = 3.17) hippocampi in TLE showed significantly greater volume reduction over time (both p < 0.05). Furthermore, annual ipsilateral hippocampal volume reduction was significantly correlated with disease duration (Spearman's rs = 0.366, FDR-corrected p = 0.036), suggesting that hippocampal atrophy progresses more rapidly during the early stage after epilepsy onset. These findings indicate that hippocampal volume loss in TLE exceeds that expected from normal aging and provide further evidence supporting progressive structural alterations during the course of the disease. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Temporal lobe epilepsy may cause progressive changes in the brain beyond those expected from normal aging. Using repeated MRI scans, we found that the hippocampus showed greater volume loss over time in people with temporal lobe epilepsy than in healthy individuals. This volume loss occurred bilaterally and appeared to be greater during the earlier stages of the disease. These results provide further evidence supporting progressive structural brain changes in TLE and contribute to a better understanding of disease progression and abnormal brain aging in epilepsy.

title: Newly diagnosed and relapsed follicular lymphoma: EHA Clinical Practice Guidelines for diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up.
abstract: Follicular lymphoma (FL) is the second most common lymphoma subtype in Europe, with a median age at diagnosis of 60-65 years. It is generally considered an indolent disease, and the median overall survival at diagnosis now likely exceeds 20 years. However, considerable heterogeneity exists. Diagnosis requires adequate biopsy material and a specialized hematopathologist. Staging and prognosis rely on positron emission tomography (PET)-computed tomography (CT). Prognostication at diagnosis is based on several validated clinical prognostic scores. Localized disease is usually treated with radiotherapy ± Rituximab. The treatment of disseminated disease includes active surveillance (or in selected cases Rituximab monotherapy) for low-tumor burden patients, and most often immunochemotherapy (or in selected cases chemo-free therapeutic options), ±antibody maintenance in high-tumor burden patients. For relapsed or refractory disease, treatment with Rituximab-Lenalidomide combination ± Tafasitamab or Epcoritamab from the first relapse and single-agent bispecific antibodies, chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy (CAR-T) cells, and Zanubrutinib-Obinutuzumab after second relapse should be prioritized over immunochemotherapy. Given the long natural history and risk of relapse, careful follow-up is an important part of patient management. Patients should be actively involved in decision-making. In this guideline, we present current evidence-based recommendations for diagnosis, staging, treatment, and follow-up.

title: Longitudinal Ultrasonographic Appearance of an Atypical Tendinous Variant of Popliteal Artery Entrapment Syndrome in an Adolescent.
abstract: A 15-year-old boy presented with left fifth-toe ulceration, claudication, and rest pain. Computed tomography angiography demonstrated proximal-to-mid popliteal artery occlusion. Duplex ultrasonography revealed thrombotic occlusion and a slender tendon crossing the artery, which appeared more conspicuous longitudinally than transversely. Magnetic resonance imaging showed apparent continuity with the main tendon of the medial head of the gastrocnemius, supporting an atypical variant of popliteal artery entrapment syndrome. Surgery was declined. At 3 months, the ulcer had healed, and symptoms improved during medical therapy, although perfusion indices remained abnormal. Longitudinal ultrasonography may facilitate delineation of slender compressive tendons.

title: Integrated Bedside Hemodynamic Assessment and Monitoring of Venous Congestion With Venous Excess Ultrasound (VExUS): A Narrative Review.
abstract: This review evaluates the venous excess ultrasound (VExUS) score as a bedside tool for quantifying systemic venous congestion and predicting congestive end-organ injury, particularly acute kidney injury (AKI). By assessing flow patterns in the hepatic, portal, and renal veins alongside inferior vena cava (IVC) size, VExUS enables serial monitoring of congestion trajectories. While highly prognostic in heart failure, its predictive performance varies in more heterogeneous populations. Ultimately, integrating VExUS with cardiac output indices may help clinicians identify specific hemodynamic phenotypes, guiding targeted, individualized therapeutic strategies.

title: An Echocardiogram-Based Ultrasound Radiomic Model Predicts Recovery of Coronary Artery Diameter in Kawasaki Disease.
abstract: Objective To develop a predictive model based on echocardiogram-based ultrasound radiomic features for the recovery of coronary artery diameter in Kawasaki disease (KD) with coronary artery lesions (CALs). Methods A total of 206 children with acute KD and left CALs who underwent coronary ultrasound before and 8 weeks after treatment were retrospectively enrolled. The patients were randomly divided into training and testing sets at a 7:3 ratio. Ultrasound radiomic features were extracted from regions of interest delineated along the coronary artery wall on pretreatment ultrasound images. Machine learning models based on five different algorithms, including logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), random forest, extra trees, and light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM), were established to predict the recovery of coronary artery diameter. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the diagnostic efficiency of the models, and the area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were calculated. Decision curve analysis (DCA) was used to evaluate the clinical benefits of the use of the models. Results Based on Z score normalization of coronary artery diameters, diameters returned to normal in 77 patients in the training set and 37 in the testing set, whereas 67 and 25 patients, respectively, showed no such recovery after treatment. A total of 1562 ultrasound radiomic features were extracted; following the use of feature selection processes, 9 optimally performing features were employed for machine learning model development. The LightGBM model showed the best diagnostic performance, with an AUC, sensitivity, and specificity of 0.867 (95% CI: 0.811-0.923), 59.7%, and 97.0%, respectively, in the training set and of 0.857 (95% CI: 0.756-0.958), 86.5%, and 76.0%, respectively, in the testing set. DCA revealed that over a threshold range of 0.4 ~ 0.8, the model offers good clinical benefits. Conclusion Machine learning models can predict the recovery of coronary artery diameter in KD and thus may offer important value for clinical decision-making.

title: Early Oral Gastrografin Followed by Immediate CT for Precise Leak Localization and Surgical Planning After Total Laryngectomy.
abstract: Purpose Pharyngocutaneous fistula (PCF) is the most common and clinically significant complication following total laryngectomy, often leading to delayed recovery and increased morbidity. Accurate and early detection of pharyngeal leak is critical; however, conventional imaging modalities such as contrast swallow studies and computed tomography (CT) have limitations in precise anatomical localization. Materials and methods This retrospective cohort study included 117 patients who underwent total laryngectomy between January 2020 and December 2025. Patients were divided into two groups according to the postoperative imaging protocol: Gastrografin swallow followed by immediate CT (Gastrografin-CT group, n = 22) and conventional imaging ( n = 95). Leak localization was assessed using a four-point ordinal scale, and surgically actionable localization was defined as a score ≥ 2. Clinical outcomes and impact on management were also evaluated. Results The Gastrografin-CT protocol demonstrated significantly improved leak localization compared with conventional imaging (mean localization score: 3.00 ± 0.00 vs. 1.62 ± 0.83, p = 0.01). Surgically actionable localization was achieved in all patients in the Gastrografin-CT group compared with 51.2% in the conventional group ( p = 0.03). Leaks were identified on initial imaging in 100% of patients in the Gastrografin-CT group versus 82.9% in the conventional group. Although clinical outcomes, including time to oral feeding, complication rates, and hospital stay, did not significantly differ, the Gastrografin-CT protocol provided more precise anatomical delineation, facilitating targeted surgical planning. Conclusion Performing CT immediately after an oral Gastrografin swallow significantly improves anatomical localization of pharyngeal leaks following total laryngectomy. By integrating leak detection and anatomical delineation in a single imaging session, this protocol enhances surgical decision-making and may serve as a practical adjunct for postoperative evaluation and management of PCF. Level of evidence 3.

title: Automated Magnetic Resonance Volumetry to Measure Multiple System Atrophy Disease Progression in Clinical Trials.
abstract: Background Recent studies have reported longitudinal brain atrophy in multiple system atrophy (MSA) in relatively small patient cohorts. Objective To compare longitudinal regional brain volume and clinical changes as endpoint measures for MSA clinical trials. Methods MSA patients with 1-year longitudinal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were selected from the placebo arm of the M-STAR Study (NCT03952806) and stratified into MSA-cerebellar (MSA-C) and MSA-parkinsonism (MSA-P) subtypes. A multisite healthy control (HC) cohort from international datasets was included for comparison. Baseline and longitudinal atrophy were assessed through automated MRI volumetry. Standardized longitudinal effect size values with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and sample sizes required to detect treatment effect were estimated for 42 individual regional brain volumes, four combined volumetric indexes, nine clinical scales, and serum neurofilament light chain. Results The final study cohort included 129 MSA patients (76 MSA-C, 53 MSA-P) and 184 HC. The most atrophic structures at baseline were infratentorial regions in MSA-C and putamen in MSA-P. In both subtypes, infratentorial structures showed the largest longitudinal volume loss compared with HC. The annualized change of a cerebellum-pons-putamen volumetric index was the most powerful progression biomarker in MSA patients (effect size: -1.81 [95% CI: -2.14, -1.55]) and in both subtypes (MSA-C: -2.04 [95% CI: -2.58, -1.68], MSA-P: -1.55 [95% CI: -2.08, -1.22]), requiring the lowest sample size per arm (MSA, N = 55 to detect 30% treatment effect), and outperforming clinical measures (-59.6% patients required per arm). Conclusion These findings support longitudinal MRI-derived regional atrophy rates as sensitive imaging endpoints to assess treatment efficacy in MSA clinical trials. © 2026 The Author(s). title: NR-MRC: A No-Reference Magnetic Resonance Curve Estimation Network for Tumor MR Image Quality Assessment and Enhancement.
abstract: Purpose Accurate image quality assessment (IQA) is essential for evaluating tumor magnetic resonance (MR) images in clinical practice and computer-aided diagnosis. However, most existing IQA models are designed for natural images and require reference images for training. Variability in tissue characteristics, lesion location, and lesion morphology, together with the scarcity of high-quality MR reference images, makes quality assessment of tumor MR images particularly challenging. Methods To address these challenges, we propose a no-reference magnetic resonance curve estimation network named NR-MRC. First, a magnetic resonance curve estimation module uses nonlinear curve mapping to estimate spatially adjusted intensity and detail features without requiring reference tumor MR images. Second, a multi-scale feature estimation module extracts contextual features at different scales and fuses them with the initial estimates to generate enhanced MR images. Finally, a magnetic resonance scene statistics blind quality model evaluates feature consistency between the original images and their enhanced counterparts. Results Experiments on publicly available brain tumor and bladder cancer datasets demonstrate that NR-MRC outperforms the compared IQA and image enhancement methods. In the tested U-Net and DeepLab v3 settings, training with images selected by high NR-MRC scores or enhanced by NR-MRC increased segmentation metrics by approximately 20%. These task-specific gains do not by themselves establish improved clinical diagnostic image quality. Conclusion NR-MRC provides no-reference quality assessment and enhancement for tumor MR images and shows potential utility in the evaluated downstream segmentation tasks.

title: Clinically suspected central nervous system Richter transformation presenting with progressive psychiatric symptoms: A case report.
abstract: Background Central nervous system (CNS) involvement associated with Richter transformation (RT) is a rare complication of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). Neurological manifestations are heterogeneous. To our knowledge, no previous reports have described CNS RT presenting predominantly with psychiatric and behavioral symptoms. We report a clinically suspected case of CNS RT presenting predominantly with progressive psychiatric symptoms in the presence of extensive CNS lesions but without apparent focal neurological deficits. Case presentation A 71-year-old man with no psychiatric history developed progressive personality change, irritability, emotional lability, behavioral disinhibition, and sleep-wake cycle disturbance. Gadolinium-enhanced fluid-attenuated inversion recovery magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated newly developed multifocal lesions predominantly involving the bilateral temporal lobes. Hematological evaluation established previously unrecognized CLL. Although histopathological confirmation was not obtained, the overall clinical, radiological, and laboratory findings supported CNS involvement associated with clinically suspected RT as the most likely diagnosis. Progressive neuropsychiatric deterioration limited invasive diagnostic procedures and disease-directed treatment. Supportive and palliative management was provided, and the patient died of aspiration pneumonia 114 days after surgery. Conclusion This case demonstrates that clinically suspected CNS RT may present predominantly with progressive psychiatric and behavioral symptoms in the absence of focal neurological deficits. Severe neuropsychiatric symptoms may themselves impede diagnostic confirmation and disease-directed treatment. When pathological confirmation is not feasible, multidisciplinary discussion and shared decision-making with the patient and family, together with explicit acknowledgment of diagnostic uncertainty and careful balancing of the benefits and burdens of further investigation and treatment, may support patient-centered care.

title: 4D-Flow MRI-Derived Wall Shear Stress as a Non-Invasive Biomarker for the Detection and Hemodynamic Characterization of Pulmonary Hypertension.
abstract: Invasive right heart catheterization (RHC) remains the reference standard for diagnosing pulmonary hypertension (PH), but there is a pressing need for non-invasive techniques to assess pulmonary hemodynamics. This study evaluates 4D-flow MRI-derived wall shear stress (WSS) for PH detection using the updated 2022 hemodynamic criteria, and the prediction of right ventriculo-pulmonary arterial (RV-PA) uncoupling to assess disease severity. 3D WSS was measured in the main (MPA), right (RPA), and left (LPA) pulmonary arteries in a retrospective validation cohort (41 PH patients, 23 non-PH) and then assessed in a prospective test cohort (23 PH patients, 17 healthy controls). For methodological validation, a patient-specific computational fluid dynamics (CFD) was performed in a subset of 16 patients from the validation cohort. RV-PA uncoupling was assessed on the cine MRI, using RV global longitudinal strain (GLS) < -15.3% and RVSV/RVESV < 1. Both 3D peak and time-averaged WSS were significantly reduced in PH patients compared with healthy controls. Global WSS metrics demonstrated the strongest correlations with invasive hemodynamic parameters, including mPAP ( r = -0.75, p < 0.001) and PVR ( r = -0.76, p < 0.001). ROC curve analysis identified a peak WSS cutoff of < 0.30 Pa (AUC 0.98) for PH detection, a threshold achieving 90% sensitivity and 100% specificity in the test cohort. Furthermore, a peak WSS threshold of < 0.18 Pa demonstrated excellent discriminative ability for RV-PA uncoupling. These findings support the potential integration of WSS analysis into routine CMR protocols as a non-invasive complement to RHC, showing promise for both diagnosis and a longitudinal biomarker for monitoring PH.

title: Discordant Cavitary Changes: A Radiological Dilemma in Invasive Mucinous Adenocarcinoma: A Case Report.
abstract: Treatment-related cavitary transformation in lung cancer may complicate radiological response assessment. We report a man in his 70s with stage IVA invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma treated with atezolizumab, bevacizumab, carboplatin and paclitaxel. After two cycles, CT showed enlargement of cavitary components despite regression of solid tumour components, making response assessment difficult. After two additional cycles, the pulmonary lesions showed little change, whereas progression of the Th4 bone metastasis led to an overall assessment of progressive disease and a change to docetaxel plus ramucirumab. Thereafter, the cavities further enlarged while the cavity walls progressively thinned and the solid components appeared to regress. This case illustrates that marked multifocal cavitary transformation may produce discordant morphological changes, limiting response assessment based on imaging alone. Serum CEA and SLX levels remained within the normal ranges at diagnosis and throughout treatment.

title: Diagnostic value of 3D pCASL perfusion in glioma grading according to the WHO 2021 classification: a retrospective study of 530 cases.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the diagnostic performance of three-dimensional pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling (3D pCASL) for preoperative grading of gliomas within the 2021 WHO classification framework and to assess protocol-specific tumor blood flow thresholds for differentiating CNS WHO grade 2 from grade 3-4 tumors. Methods This retrospective single-center study included 530 patients with newly diagnosed supratentorial glial tumors examined between 2011 and 2024. Nineteen non-diffuse CNS WHO grade 1 tumors were retained for descriptive purposes only and excluded from all grading analyses; the primary analytical cohort therefore comprised 511 gliomas (grade 2, n = 75; grade 3, n = 152; grade 4, n = 284). Diagnoses were reassigned within the WHO 2021 framework using the histological and molecular information available for each patient; tumors lacking molecular information required for an integrated WHO diagnosis were designated NOS. All patients underwent 3.0 T MRI with 3D pCASL. Maximum tumor blood flow (maxTBF) and normalized TBF relative to white matter (nTBF WM) and gray matter (nTBF GM) were measured using approximately 30-mm² hotspot ROIs. Results In gliomas, maxTBF, nTBF WM, and nTBF GM differentiated grade 2 from grade 3-4 tumors, with AUCs of 0.848, 0.833, and 0.84, respectively. The maxTBF threshold was 63.3 mL/100 g/min; AUCs were 0.743-0.768 for grade 2 versus grade 3 and 0.668-0.715 for grade 3 versus grade 4. After exclusion of NOS cases, glioblastomas and grade 4 astrocytomas did not differ significantly in maxTBF or nTBF (pfdr > 0.05). 3D pCASL also differentiated non-enhancing glioblastomas from grade 2 astrocytomas (maxTBF, pfdr = 0.0018; nTBF, pfdr = 0.0036-0.006), with AUCs of 0.78-0.86, a maxTBF cutoff of 64.1 mL/100 g/min, and specificity up to 96%. maxTBF and nTBF moderately correlated with Ki-67 (r = 0.44-0.50; pfdr < 0.001). Conclusions 3D pCASL provides high diagnostic accuracy for differentiating grade 2 gliomas from high-grade gliomas and grade 2 from grade 3 tumors within the WHO 2021 framework, while remaining fully non-invasive and requiring no contrast agent.

After exclusion of NOS cases, glioblastomas and grade 4 astrocytomas did not differ significantly in maxTBF or nTBF (pfdr > 0.05). 3D pCASL also differentiated non-enhancing glioblastomas from grade 2 astrocytomas (maxTBF, pfdr = 0.0018; nTBF, pfdr = 0.0036-0.006), with AUCs of 0.78-0.86, a maxTBF cutoff of 64.1 mL/100 g/min, and specificity up to 96%. maxTBF and nTBF moderately correlated with Ki-67 (r = 0.44-0.50; pfdr < 0.001).

Conclusions

3D pCASL provides high diagnostic accuracy for differentiating grade 2 gliomas from high-grade gliomas and grade 2 from grade 3 tumors within the WHO 2021 framework, while remaining fully non-invasive and requiring no contrast agent.

title: Thrombosed mycotic aneurysm of the cervical internal carotid artery mimicking a parapharyngeal abscess in a child: a case report of multimodal imaging diagnosis.
abstract: A parapharyngeal abscess, although relatively rare, is a potentially life-threatening deep neck space infection in the pediatric population that carries a risk of serious complications. Mycotic pseudoaneurysm of the cervical internal carotid artery (ICA) is a rare vascular complication in children that can lead to catastrophic hemorrhage if misdiagnosed and attempted for surgical incision. We report a 7-year-old malnourished boy presenting with fever, dysphagia, and neck stiffness. Suboptimal contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) suggested a left parapharyngeal abscess, and surgical drainage was planned. A dedicated CT, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) mapping, magnetic resonance angiography, and three-dimensional CT angiography identified a completely thrombosed mycotic pseudoaneurysm rather than an abscess. This case demonstrates that complete thrombosis transforms a mycotic pseudoaneurysm into a mass that can easily be mistaken for an abscess without the right imaging modalities and high-quality imaging.

title: Technique, Safety and Adoption of Genicular Artery Embolization for Knee Osteoarthritis: A Nationwide Analysis of the German Quality-Assurance Registry.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the nationwide adoption of genicular artery embolization (GAE) in Germany and to describe patient selection, technique, safety and radiation dose. Materials and methods We retrospectively analyzed procedures recorded in the quality-assurance registry of the German Society for Interventional Radiology and Minimally Invasive Therapy (DeGIR), from January 2024 to December 2025. Technical success, entered per procedure, was defined as subjective adequate devascularization of the synovial blush. Complications were graded using the modified CIRSE classification, and radiation exposure was expressed as dose-area product (DAP) and fluoroscopy time. The analysis was primarily descriptive. Results Overall, 2335 procedures in 2209 patients across 109 centers in 15 federal states were recorded (median age 67 years, IQR 59-77; 57% female; prior total knee arthroplasty (TKA) in 300, 13%). Annual volume rose from 579 procedures in 2024 to 1,756 in 2025, and the embolic agent shifted from permanent (40-21%) toward temporary microspheres (4-29%). Center-reported technical success was 93% (87% in 2024, 94% in 2025). Eleven complications were recorded (0.5%), all CIRSE grade 1-3, with no permanent sequelae; none were recorded in 2024. Median DAP was 1536 cGy cm 2 (IQR 731-3048) and median fluoroscopy time 24 min (IQR 16-34). Conclusion During rapid nationwide adoption, GAE was performed for osteoarthritis-related and post-TKA pain with low radiation dose and high center-reported technical success across centers of all volumes, supporting its feasibility in routine practice. The complication rate is a lower limit, as the registry is not designed for complication surveillance.

title: [Cardiac involvement in idiopathic inflammatory myopathies].
abstract: Background Cardiac manifestations in idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) occur more frequently than they are clinically recognized and are associated with increased morbidity and mortality. In particular, subclinical myocarditis often remains undetected due to nonspecific or absent symptoms. Objective This review aims to summarize the prevalence, pathophysiology, clinical spectrum, diagnostic strategies and therapeutic options of cardiac involvement in IIM and to provide practical recommendations for rheumatologists. Methods A scoping review on cardiac manifestations in IIM was performed. A structured literature search was conducted using the PubMed database. The search strategy included combinations of relevant keywords and MeSH terms. Primarily, English language original studies, systematic reviews and current guideline publications related to cardiac involvement in IIM were considered. Studies were selected based on clinical relevance, methodological quality and recency. Results The reported prevalence of cardiac involvement in IIM ranges from 4-26%, depending on the subtype and diagnostic approach. In addition to clinically overt myocarditis, subclinical abnormalities are common and can be detected in up to 50% of patients using cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI). Pathophysiological mechanisms include immune-mediated myocardial injury, microvascular dysfunction and fibrotic remodelling. The initial diagnostic work-up should comprise taking a medical history, electrocardiography, measurement of cardiac biomarkers and echocardiography. The use of CMRI represents the diagnostic gold standard and enables sensitive detection of inflammatory and fibrotic myocardial changes. Therapeutically, early initiation of drug treatment, typically high-dose glucocorticoids combined with additional immunomodulating agents, constitutes the cornerstone of management. Conclusion Cardiac manifestations in IIM are common, prognostically relevant and frequently underestimated in clinical practice. A structured diagnostic approach with early use of CMRI and interdisciplinary management is essential to detect subclinical disease and guide appropriate treatment.

title: Validation of 3D intraoral scanner use for detecting caries lesions around dental restorations: A diagnostic accuracy study.
abstract: Objectives This study aimed to validate the use of a 3D intraoral scanner (IOS) for detecting secondary caries lesions around restorations using image-based CARS-derived severity categories, compared with visual-tactile clinical examination. Materials and methods A diagnostic validation study was conducted at the university clinical facilities, from July 2023 to September 2024, including adult patients with amalgam or composite resin restorations on anterior and posterior teeth. The restorations were assessed using visual-tactile clinical examination, adopted as the clinical reference standard, and IOS image-based assessment. Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, binary-classification AUC, and clinical-IOS agreement were estimated. Confidence intervals for diagnostic accuracy measures were obtained using participant-level cluster bootstrap resampling. Results A total of 299 restorations in 41 patients were assessed. IOS sensitivity varied, with 75% (95% CI: 66.2-82.0) at the initial lesion threshold, 40% (95% CI: 20.8-57.7) at the moderate lesion threshold, and 57.1% (95% CI: 33.3-100.0) at the severe lesion threshold. Specificity was consistently high, with 84.1% (95% CI: 78.7-89.4), 97.4% (95% CI: 95.6-99.2), and 99.7% (95% CI: 98.7-99.7) at the initial, moderate, and severe lesion thresholds, respectively. Binary-classification AUC values were 0.79 (95% CI: 0.75-0.84), 0.69 (95% CI: 0.58-0.78), and 0.78 (95% CI: 0.66-1.00) at the initial, moderate, and severe lesion thresholds, respectively. Positive predictive value was highest at the severe lesion threshold (80%), while the negative predictive value was especially high at this threshold (99%). Exact clinical-IOS agreement was 77.9%, whereas linearly weighted observed agreement was 91.1%, with a linearly weighted kappa coefficient of 0.53. Conclusions The 3D intraoral scanner is a complementary tool for assessing secondary caries lesions, showing high specificity across lesion thresholds. Sensitivity varied according to lesion severity and was less precise at the severe threshold due to the small number of severe lesions. Future research should increase sample sizes and explore combining IOS with other diagnostic methods to improve detection, especially for moderate lesions and higher caries prevalence. Clinical relevance Conventional IOS images may assist in documenting and assessing visible changes around restorations. Clinical interpretation should consider the observed sensitivity limitations and incorporate visual-tactile examination and radiographic assessment when indicated.

title: Cerebrospinal fluid positive for SARS-CoV-2 associated with neurological manifestations and proteome alterations in a multiple myeloma patient.
abstract: Background Although SARS-CoV-2 infection is primarily associated with respiratory symptoms, neurological complications have been increasingly recognized, even in the absence of pulmonary involvement. Case presentation We report a case of a 67-year-old woman with a history of multiple myeloma and recent exposure to a COVID-19-positive individual who developed rapidly progressive neurological symptoms, including dysarthria, dysphagia, and hypoesthesia, without any respiratory manifestations. Her condition deteriorated to focal and dyscognitive status epilepticus, requiring mechanical ventilation. Brain MRI showed imaging features consistent with rhombencephalitis. SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed through positive qRT-PCR results from both nasopharyngeal swab and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Further analysis of the CSF using quantitative shotgun proteomics via mass spectrometry revealed a neuroinflammatory profile indicative of blood-brain barrier disruption and differential expression of several proteins relevant to brain function, including the major prion protein, superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD-1), and other aggregation-prone proteins. Conclusions This case supports the hypothesis that SARS-CoV-2 can invade the central nervous system and cause severe neurological impairment, even in the absence of typical respiratory symptoms. The findings underscore the importance of considering SARS-CoV-2 in the differential diagnosis of rapidly progressive neurological syndromes and highlight the need for further investigation into the mechanisms of neuroinvasion and the potential neurotropism of emerging viral variants.

title: A comprehensive analysis of the association of psychological profiling and sagittal balance parameters with neck pain in a non-deformity cervical spondylosis population: A prospective two-centers cross-sectional study.
abstract: Purpose to comprehensively identify determining factors of perceived neck pain in a non-deformity population, integrating psychological and sagittal balance parameters.Methods a cross-sectional study of prospectively collected data was conducted on patients admitted for cervical spondylosis at two tertiary university hospitals between April 2024 and August 2025. Eligible cases were retrieved from the PANDA Registry. Records were excluded if standing X-ray was unavailable and/or not-evaluable (e.g. shoulder prosthesis); or if the admission pathology involved the cranio-cervical junction, tumors, deformities, spinal cord disease, or infections. Preoperative data included demographic, clinical (VAS neck), psychological (SCL-27, I-TIPI, CD-RISC10), and sagittal balance variables (McGregor slope, C1-C2 lordosis, C2 slope, C2-C7 lordosis, cSVA, T1 slope, cervical mismatch). Correction for multiple comparisons was applied within pre-specified hypothesis domains.Results one-hundred-thirty records were included. Intra-rater reliability for radiographic parameters was excellent (> 0.9). After categorization of patients by neck pain severity, pairwise analysis showed that only C1-C2 lordosis remained significantly higher in patients exhibiting severe neck pain (VAS < 7 vs. VAS ≥ 7). When stratified for moderate-to-severe neck pain (VAS ≥ 4), several SCL-27 scales, namely dysthymic, vegetative, agoraphobic, sociophobic, and GSI scores, and C1C2 lordosis showed significant differences. Correlation analysis using VAS neck as the dependent variable demonstrated a significant positive correlation with SCL-27 dysthymic and vegetative scores. C1-C2 lordosis showed a significant inverse correlation with neck pain. In univariate analysis, only SCL-27 dysthymic, vegetative, and GSI scores emerged as significant univariate associations of VAS neck. After correction for multiple comparisons, the SCL-27 vegetative, dysthymic and GSI scores retained significance, whereas C1-C2 lordosis did not.Conclusion in a non-deformity population, sagittal balance parameters alone do not adequately explain patient-perceived neck pain. These findings support the preoperative use of psychological assessments, especially the SCL-27, as a useful tool in preoperative screening and individualised counselling.

title: BLIX-Ray: Chest X-Ray Report Generation with Vision-Language Models and Reinforcement Learning.
abstract: The radiology report is essential for directing the course of treatment for a patient. However, writing radiology reports is a huge burden for radiologists. Manual reporting faces challenges due to intra-labeler and inter-labeler variability, causing inconsistent patient treatment and diagnostic results, and complicating matters due to alertness and changing judgment. To address these challenges, we propose an automated radiology report generation model tailored for chest X-ray imaging. We introduce BLIX-Ray, a vision-language model (VLM) designed to generate radiology reports using a transfer learning approach. BLIX-Ray fine-tunes the pre-trained BLIP model to extract and align rich visual and textual representations suited to the medical imaging domain. We use reinforcement learning (RL) to directly optimize report generation based on language evaluation metrics in order to further enhance performance. We evaluate BLIX-Ray on two publicly available datasets: IU-Xray and CheXpert Plus. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves the highest CIDEr and BERTScore on both datasets, while n-gram-oriented baselines retain an advantage on BLEU. BLIX-Ray integrates reinforcement learning and transfer learning to improve medical report generation under limited and heterogeneous data conditions. The results highlight the potential of vision-language models to support automated and standardized radiology reporting. Notably, BLIX-Ray achieves the best reported CIDEr (0.6534) and BERTScore (0.8765) among the compared methods on IU-Xray and leads on CIDEr, METEOR, and BERTScore on CheXpert Plus (BERTScore 0.8407), demonstrating strong report-level consensus and semantic similarity with the reference reports.

title: Annotation-Efficient Individual Muscle Segmentation from Dixon MRI: A Multi-Dataset Benchmark of Pretraining and Fat-Fraction Guidance.
abstract: Measuring individual muscles and their fatty infiltration on Dixon MRI can support sarcopenia assessment, but manual annotation is time-consuming and annotated datasets are often small. This study investigated accurate individual-muscle segmentation with limited labelled data. Three datasets were used: an abdominal CT dataset of 300 subjects with adipose-tissue labels, a lower-limb Dixon MRI dataset of 25 subjects with 13 thigh and 9 calf muscles, and an independent cohort of 66 subjects for external testing. Network architecture, encoder pretraining, a Dixon-derived fat-fraction input, and a shared CT-MRI encoder were compared. A 2.5D model, subject-level cross-validation, zero-shot transfer, label-free domain adaptation, and few-shot adaptation were also evaluated. The best models reached Dice 0.947±0.017 for CT adipose tissue and 0.925±0.010 for thigh muscle; the best 2.5D model reached 0.928, while a reported 3D Attention-Res-V-Net reached 0.857 under a different protocol. Encoder pretraining helped most at the smallest budgets, with ImageNet performing best and comparably to CT-based pretraining at eight subjects. A shared CT-MRI encoder retained accuracy with 44% fewer parameters, and thigh-muscle volumes agreed closely with reference measurements (ICC (2,1)=0.998 ). On the external cohort, fine-tuning raised Dice from 0.11 zero-shot to 0.61, 0.76, and 0.88 with four, eight, and 46 labelled target subjects. The fat-fraction input improved segmentation only when very few subjects (two or four) were labelled. Encoder pretraining and efficient model sharing help when annotated MRI data are scarce. A small amount of target-domain annotation substantially improves cross-cohort transfer, and repeated subject-level validation is important for reliable evaluation.

title: Automated Multi-class Segmentation of Mandibular Odontogenic Cysts and the Mandibular Canal on CBCT Images Using a Hybrid Deep Learning Framework.
abstract: Mandibular odontogenic cysts can complicate surgical planning if located near the mandibular canal. Accurate delineation of both structures is therefore clinically important. This study presents a deep learning-based method for simultaneously segmenting mandibular odontogenic cysts and the mandibular canal in cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) images. The developed method relies on a hybrid deep learning architecture integrating a ConvNeXt-Base encoder, a Dilated Context Block, a U-Net-based decoder, and a Deep Supervision mechanism. This framework simultaneously segments the mandibular canal and odontogenic cyst regions within the same architecture, promoting multi-scale contextual feature learning. We evaluated the performance of the proposed method using fivefold cross-validation experiments on a real-world clinical CBCT dataset comprising 103 patient images. We assessed segmentation performance using overlap-based metrics together with boundary-aware HD95 and ASSD metrics. The experimental results demonstrated that the model achieved a mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 76.28% ± 1.83%. Excluding the background class yielded macro IoU and macro F1-score values of 64.46% ± 2.74% and 77.00% ± 1.89%, respectively. Meanwhile, the weighted IoU and weighted F1-score values were 78.71% ± 4.25% and 87.63% ± 2.63%, respectively. In boundary-based evaluations, the mandibular canal had an HD95 of 2.44 ± 2.98 mm and an ASSD of 0.45 ± 0.30 mm. The corresponding values for odontogenic cysts were 5.59 ± 3.65 mm and 1.43 ± 0.88 mm, respectively. These results suggest that the mandibular canal is more consistently delineated, while cyst segmentation remains more challenging, particularly at irregular and low-contrast boundaries. The proposed framework allows for the simultaneous and objective segmentation of mandibular odontogenic cysts and the mandibular canal within a unified, multi-class CBCT analysis framework. By providing reproducible delineation of both structures, this method could serve as a technical foundation for future quantitative analyses of lesion-canal relationships. However, further validation using larger, multicenter, volumetric CBCT datasets is required before clinical translation.

title: Impact of Field Strength and Contrast Agents on Cardiac MRI Radiomic Features of the Myocardium and Blood Pool.
abstract: The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of gadolinium-based contrast agents on cardiac MRI radiomic features across different magnetic field strengths. With Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval, eight healthy volunteers (38.5 ± 15.4 years; 4 males) underwent four consecutive cardiac MRI examinations using a Modified Look-Locker Inversion Recovery (MOLLI) sequence at 1.5T and 3T, with and without two contrast agents, gadopentetate dimeglumine (Gd-DTPA), and gadofosveset trisodium. Radiomic features were extracted from the myocardium and blood pool at the mid-ventricular level of the left ventricle using the first raw MOLLI image, corresponding to the shortest inversion time. Before contrast administration, switching from 1.5 to 3 T resulted in significant changes in 52% of myocardial and 56% of blood pool radiomic features. Contrast administration further altered radiomic feature values. At 1.5T, Gd-DTPA altered 42% of myocardial and 63% of blood pool features, whereas gadofosveset altered 73% and 85%, respectively. Similar patterns were observed at 3 T, with gadofosveset producing a greater proportion of altered features than Gd-DTPA (p < 0.05). Blood pool features were generally more sensitive to contrast administration than myocardial features. At 10 min after contrast administration, significant differences between the two contrast agents were observed in 48% of myocardial and 23% of blood pool features at 1.5T and in 72% and 60%, respectively, at 3 T. In conclusion, the administration and type of gadolinium-based contrast agents significantly alter cardiac MRI radiomic features across different magnetic field strengths. Future research should prioritize normalization strategies and evaluate feature robustness across larger patient populations to enhance the generalizability of cardiac radiomics.

title: SVF-net: A Dual-encoder Network with Adaptive Gated Fusion for Colorectal Polyp Segmentation.
abstract: Automatic colorectal polyp segmentation in retrospective still colonoscopy images remains challenging for small, low-contrast, partially occluded, or irregular lesions. We propose SVF-Net, a heterogeneous dual-encoder network combining a frozen SAM2 Hiera-L image trunk with a trainable MaxViT-RMLP-Small specialist branch. At four feature scales, the two streams are projected to a common width, spatially aligned, and reconciled by complementary channel-spatial gating before progressive decoding. Across five public benchmarks, three-run mean mDice is 0.922 on CVC-ClinicDB, 0.898 on Kvasir-SEG, 0.805 on CVC-ColonDB, 0.770 on ETIS-LaribPolypDB, and 0.896 on CVC-300. Matched projected-concatenation and fixed-weight ( G=0.5 ) controls retain the surrounding fusion path while removing input-dependent weighting; across ten matched training runs, adaptive gating gives higher mean mDice than both controls on all five datasets. Dataset-wide gate diagnostics on all 380 CVC-ColonDB and 196 ETIS cases indicate non-collapsed, scale- and region-dependent activations, while targeted one-factor sensitivity checks cover the MaxViT learning-rate multiplier, gate initialization, and auxiliary-loss weight. Matched per-case analyses further show that cross-domain gains are heterogeneous across lesion size, brightness, and an image-derived specular-reflection proxy. SVF-Net requires 92.8 ms per image (10.8 FPS) and 8.5 GB peak GPU memory on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 under the reported profiling protocol. The study evaluates retrospective static images only and does not establish real-time colonoscopy performance, prospective clinical effectiveness, or clinician benefit.

title: PW-GAN: Pseudo-Warping Field Guided GAN for Unsupervised Denoising of Fetal Brain MRI Images.
abstract: Fetal brain MRI commonly uses thick-slice acquisitions to mitigate motion artifacts and preserve in-plane image quality. Multiple motion-corrupted stacks of 2D slices can be retrospectively reconstructed into isotropic 3D volumes; however, volumes reconstructed from thicker slices generally exhibit lower image quality than those reconstructed from thinner slices because limited through-plane information results in residual noise and inter-slice structural discontinuities. Existing post-reconstruction denoising methods are limited by their dependence on large-scale datasets comprising noisy-clean image pairs or insufficient modeling of inter-slice structural consistency. In this work, we propose a Pseudo-Warping Field Guided Unsupervised Generative Adversarial Network (PW-GAN), which formulates post-reconstruction denoising as unpaired translation between low- and high-quality MRI domains. By incorporating a pseudo-warping field module, our method significantly enhances inter-slice continuity in the reconstructed volumes while effectively suppressing residual noise and inter-slice structural discontinuities. On simulated data, PW-GAN achieved a PSNR of 39.65 dB and an SSIM of 0.9932. On real clinical data, it reduced the inter-slice warping error by up to 40% compared with unsupervised baselines. These results demonstrate that PW-GAN outperforms existing unsupervised models and achieves performance comparable to several state-of-the-art supervised methods. Qualitatively, PW-GAN produced cleaner results with smoother inter-slice structural transitions while preserving anatomical structures, demonstrating its effectiveness in post-reconstruction denoising of fetal brain MRI acquired from thick-slice scans.
